company.name: Thalvik
company.one_liner: Thalvik sells mid-market finance teams a combined corporate-card, invoice-capture and automatic-coding layer that writes continuously to the ERP so the monthly close no longer requires manual reconciliation.

overview: Thalvik is a Copenhagen-based, seed-stage (founded April 2024, 11 people) spend-management startup raising EUR 3.5M at an EUR 18M pre-money valuation, with EUR 1.2M soft-circled from two Nordic funds. It sells a card-issuance + invoice-capture + automatic ledger-coding product to mid-market companies (150-1,500 employees) in the Nordics, DACH and Benelux, and reports EUR 41,300 software MRR plus EUR 9,100 monthly interchange across 34 paying customers as of 30 November 2025. The core wedge claimed is a per-tenant coding engine that proposes ledger accounts/cost centres automatically, differentiating it from card-only or ERP-native alternatives. Independent research could not corroborate the deck's market-size figures, competitive claims, or either founder's professional history; a well-known, well-funded direct competitor (Pleo) headquartered in the same city is entirely absent from the deck's competition slide.

tam_sam_som.tam_stated: USD 48B — global spend management and B2B expense software, all company sizes, 2025
tam_sam_som.sam_stated: USD 6.2B — companies of 150-1,500 employees in Nordics, DACH and Benelux, ~61,000 companies at blended USD 102k ACV
tam_sam_som.som_stated: USD 2.9B within three years — annualised revenue and interchange across the SAM by end of year three
tam_sam_som.summary: The deck shows a top-down TAM (Gartner category revenue plus an interchange pool add-on) and a bottom-up SAM (company count x blended ACV), which is a reasonable structure for pre-seed. However, the SOM of USD 2.9B against a SAM of USD 6.2B implies capturing roughly 47% of the entire addressable market within three years from a base of EUR 41k MRR today — an extreme and effectively unsupported jump that sits far outside a credible 1-15% band, so it is flagged. None of the headline TAM/SAM/SOM figures, nor the Gartner category definition, nor the PSD2/e-invoicing 'why now' claims, could be independently verified in this research pass (the search budget was exhausted before these checks ran) — this is a verification gap, not a confirmation or refutation, and should be treated as unresolved rather than accepted at face value.

competitors.name: SAP Concur
competitors.differentiation_claimed: Deck claims Concur is enterprise-focused, 6-9 month implementation starting around EUR 60k, no card issuance, no continuous ledger write-back; Thalvik claims to win on time-to-value.

competitors.name: Legacy ERP add-on modules (Dynamics expense modules, Fortnox add-ons)
competitors.differentiation_claimed: Deck claims these are 'forms over a database' with no card, no point-of-authorisation capture, and no coding intelligence; Thalvik claims to win on 'the actual work.'

competitors.name: Spreadsheets / shared invoice mailbox
competitors.differentiation_claimed: Deck states this was present in 26 of 34 paying customers before they bought Thalvik; Thalvik claims to win because the controller's own time is the effective budget.

competitors.name: Pleo
competitors.funding_info: Reported to have secured a $43 million (EUR 40 million) debt financing facility; described as serving 30,000+ customers, well past seed stage.
competitors.differentiation_claimed: Not mentioned in the deck. External sources describe Pleo as offering physical, virtual and vendor cards plus expense/invoice management with integrations into NetSuite, Xero and QuickBooks, serving companies from startups to enterprises — directly overlapping Thalvik's stated card+invoice+ERP wedge and segment.

competitors.why_now_why_us: Deck argues timing is driven by PSD2/open-banking rails making ledger-grade transaction data available without a bank partnership, e-invoicing mandates in Germany (2025) and Belgium (2026) forcing AP-stack changes, and flat mid-market finance headcount against rising transaction volume creating budget for automation. This is more specific than a generic 'big market plus AI' pitch, citing named regulatory triggers with dates, but none of these regulatory claims were independently verified in this pass, and the 'why us' argument (a controller-CTO combining ledger closing experience with card-issuing engineering) rests entirely on unverified founder bios.
competitors.summary: The deck positions Thalvik against three groups — SAP Concur (enterprise incumbent), legacy ERP expense add-ons, and spreadsheets/shared mailboxes — and claims a differentiated 'coding intelligence' wedge that none of them addresses. None of the deck's specific competitive claims (Concur implementation time/pricing, add-on module weaknesses) could be independently verified. More importantly, research surfaced Pleo, a Copenhagen-headquartered, well-capitalized spend-management company serving the same buyer motion (cards + invoices + ERP integrations including NetSuite, Xero) across company sizes that include Thalvik's target segment, with debt financing reported at $43M and 30,000+ customers — yet Pleo is completely absent from the deck's competition slide. This is a material omission for a same-city, same-buyer-segment competitor.

categories.evidence: Deck claims CEO ran monthly close for Maersk's terminals division and CTO was a staff engineer on Klarna's card-issuing platform; no external source could confirm either claim, and named-search attempts for both individuals returned no matches.

Deck articulates a specific wedge (continuous, tenant-specific coding vs. commoditised card issuance) and a clear reason competitors haven't solved it, but this is entirely self-asserted with no external validation of the stated competitive gap.
No independently verifiable prior startup, product-launch, or exit history is given or found for either founder beyond the claimed corporate roles, which are themselves unverified.
Deck provides no evidence (e.g., pivots, cross-functional moves) bearing on this category, and no external source fills the gap.

Deck states the CEO led a spend-policy rollout across 14 country entities at Maersk and that two engineers followed the CTO from her previous company, which if true suggests some leadership pull, but neither claim could be externally confirmed.

Deck states 6 signed LOIs from accounting firms and an advisor (a partner at a Copenhagen accounting firm) who introduced the first four customers, plus EUR 1.2M soft-circled from two Nordic funds — these are concrete, named deck facts suggesting an active network, though the LOIs and soft-circle amounts are self-reported and not externally verified.
No evidence in the deck or research bearing on how the founders have handled prior setbacks.

Deck reports founder-led sales closing all 34 paying customers, 11% average MoM MRR growth over six months, and a live product with native integrations into four accounting systems plus a NetSuite private beta — concrete, specific execution evidence, albeit self-reported and not externally audited.

founder_profile.summary: Both founders have plausible, complementary backgrounds as described in the deck — a controller-turned-CEO with claimed Maersk group-finance experience and a payments engineer CTO with a claimed Klarna card-issuing background — which if true would be a strong founder-market-fit story. However, independent research could not confirm either founder's identity, employment history, or degree via any public source; searches for both named individuals returned no matching profiles, only unrelated people with similar names. This means the founder narrative currently rests entirely on the deck's own assertions with zero external corroboration, which is a material gap for a story where founder-market fit is the headline argument.

additional_metrics.name: problem_validation
additional_metrics.summary: Deck cites 40 structured discovery interviews (March-September 2025) with Nordic and German controllers, producing specific findings (6-9 days/month on reconciliation, 18% of card transactions missing receipts at 30 days, 3 of 40 companies found duplicate subscription spend above EUR 100k at audit). This is a reasonably specific and sized qualitative validation exercise for pre-seed, though it is entirely self-reported and unaudited.

additional_metrics.name: traction
additional_metrics.summary: Deck reports EUR 41,300 software MRR plus EUR 9,100 interchange, 34 paying customers, 11% average MoM growth over six months, 71% weekly active rate, 4.1% monthly logo churn, and 106% net revenue retention. These are specific, multi-dimensional figures, but all are self-reported with no external audit or investor-verifiable source, and the median close-time improvement (9.5 to 4.0 days) is explicitly flagged in the deck itself as self-reported by the controller.

additional_metrics.name: business_model_clarity
additional_metrics.summary: Pricing is clearly stated (EUR 14/employee/month with EUR 490 floor, plus 0.40% interchange take), and a median contract value (EUR 1,215 MRR) is given. However, the SAM build uses a blended USD 102k annual contract value across ~61,000 companies, which is roughly 7x the deck's own stated median contract of EUR 1,215 MRR (~EUR 14,580/year) — the price used in the TAM/SAM build does not appear to reconcile with the price the company actually charges today, and the deck does not explain the gap (e.g. whether it assumes much larger accounts or full interchange capture at maturity).

additional_metrics.name: cap_table_legal
additional_metrics.summary: Cap table shows founders holding 71% (Mikkel 38%, Aino 33%), option pool 9% (6% granted), pre-seed angels 8%, and notably 12% held in common stock by the first advisor from a 2024 arrangement made 'before we had counsel.' A 12% stake to a single advisor, granted without legal counsel involved, is an unusually large and procedurally risky allocation that a lead investor will need to examine closely — it could complicate the cap table, trigger renegotiation, or signal weak early governance discipline.

additional_metrics.name: ask_and_use_of_funds
additional_metrics.summary: The EUR 3.5M ask against 22 months of runway is allocated 45% engineering, 30% GTM, 15% compliance/licensing, 10% G&A, and is tied to concrete milestones (EUR 250k MRR by month 18, 40 accounting-firm partners, SOC2 + EMI licence). This is a coherent structure, but the 15% compliance allocation for an own EMI licence may understate the cost: external research on Danish EMI licensing indicates a EUR 350,000 statutory minimum initial capital requirement under EMD2, which the deck's compliance/licensing budget line does not explicitly address or reconcile against.

additional_metrics.name: non_obvious_insight
additional_metrics.summary: The deck's framing that the buyer compares Thalvik's price to 'half an accountant' (EUR 2,600/month in Denmark) rather than to other software, and that this framing enabled two list-price increases in 14 months with no measurable close-rate impact, is a specific and somewhat contrarian pricing insight rather than a generic market thesis. It is self-reported but concrete and testable against the founder in a meeting.

key_findings.title: Deck omits Pleo, a same-city, well-funded direct competitor
key_findings.explanation: The competition slide names SAP Concur, generic ERP add-ons, and spreadsheets, but omits Pleo, a Copenhagen-headquartered spend-management company that external sources describe as offering card issuance, invoice/expense management and NetSuite/Xero integrations to companies from startups to enterprises, with reported debt financing of $43M and 30,000+ customers.
key_findings.why_it_matters: If a well-capitalized, same-city, same-buyer competitor is left off the competitive slide, the investor cannot trust the deck's competitive positioning at face value, and needs to understand directly from the founders why Pleo is not treated as a threat.

key_findings.title: SOM implies capturing ~47% of the stated SAM within three years
key_findings.explanation: The deck's SOM (USD 2.9B within three years) against its own stated SAM (USD 6.2B) implies capturing roughly 47% of the entire addressable market from a current base of ~EUR 50k combined monthly revenue, with no bridging model shown for how accountant-channel distribution gets there.
key_findings.why_it_matters: A SOM this large a share of SAM this fast is not a credible base case and suggests the market-sizing slide was built to produce an impressive top-line number rather than a defensible bottom-up plan; the investor should press for the actual bridge (customer count, ACV, channel conversion rate) behind the year-three number.

key_findings.why_it_matters: If the market-sizing ACV is not reachable from the pricing model the company actually uses today, the SAM figure overstates the credible reachable revenue pool, which affects how much confidence the investor should place in the market-size slide.

founder_questions.question: We could not find any public record (LinkedIn, press, alumni listings) confirming your prior roles at Maersk or Klarna. Can you walk us through your specific dates of employment, manager names, and a reference we could speak to at each company?

Pleo is headquartered in Copenhagen, serves the same 150-1,500 employee segment, and already offers card issuance plus NetSuite/Xero integration. Why is Pleo not on your competitive slide, and specifically, why can't Pleo build the same tenant-specific coding model you're describing as your wedge?

Your SAM assumes a blended USD 102k annual contract value, but your current median customer pays EUR 1,215 MRR (~EUR 14.6k/year) — about a seventh of that. What specific mix of larger accounts, expanded interchange capture, or pricing changes bridges that gap, and by what year do you expect the median account to reach that level?

Your SOM implies capturing roughly half of your stated SAM within three years from today's ~EUR 50k combined monthly revenue. Walk us through the actual customer-count and channel-conversion assumptions behind that number, quarter by quarter.

The 12% advisor equity grant was made before you had legal counsel. Is that grant documented in a binding agreement today, is it subject to vesting or clawback, and has counsel now reviewed and confirmed it is enforceable as-is?
